ca_great_wall_of_china.blurb: A busy wall in the middle stretch of the Owens River Gorge, cut into hard volcanic tuff. The climbing is almost entirely bolted and steep to vertical, working pockets and flakes. Most lines fall in the 5.10 and 5.11 range, with a handful of easier ones and a few 5.12 to 5.14 test pieces, so it suits both warm-up laps and projecting. Yellow Peril, Manchurian Candidate and Tsunami are among the best-known lines. This is the most visited part of the gorge, so expect company, and take care not to knock loose rock down the gully onto people below.
ca_great_wall_of_china.parking_note: From Highway 395 about 12 miles north of Bishop, turn onto Gorge Road and bear left at the T. The middle lot, a few miles along, serves the Central Gorge; stay on the dirt shoulder away from the pavement.
ca_great_wall_of_china.approach: A steep, loose gully (class 2-3) drops from the lot to the dirt road along the river; the wall is a short walk from the bottom.

ca_lower_elbow_room.blurb: A sunny single-pitch wall in the Upper Gorge of the Owens River Gorge, on welded tuff above the creek. It faces south, which makes it a popular choice on cool days from autumn into early spring; in warmer months it heats up fast. The climbing is nearly all bolted, with grades spread from the 5.7s up through the 5.12s and the heaviest concentration at 5.10 to 5.12. Slip 'n Slide, Stinkfist and Wings are among the standouts. Getting in takes a creek crossing and a scramble up a loose talus slope, so wear shoes you can walk in.
ca_lower_elbow_room.approach: From the river road, walk a short way downstream, cross the creek, then follow a trail up loose talus to the base of the wall.

ca_1_black_wall_left.blurb: The left-hand section of Black Wall, the largest cliff on Donner Summit, a granite face that looks out over Old Highway 40. The climbing is mostly traditional, on cracks, corners and chimneys, with a few bolted lines; routes of three or four pitches are typical across the wall. Most grades sit between 5.9 and 5.11, with some 5.12 on top. One Hand Clapping, Touch and Go and Firecracker are good ones to start with. The wall is at about 7,000 feet and the walk up is steeper than it looks if you have just arrived from low elevation. Snow limits the cold months.
ca_1_black_wall_left.parking_note: Climbing the road from Donner Lake, look for a small pull-off perched above it on your right.
ca_1_black_wall_left.approach: For the left side, pick up the small trail just above the pull-off and scramble from boulder to boulder straight up the boulder field to the cliff.

ca_east_face_8.blurb: The east side of Grouse Slab, a granite slab on Donner Summit away from the main roadside crowds. It mixes easy cracks, bolted slab and a couple of two-pitch lines, so it works for beginners leading trad as well as for moderate sport climbers. Grades run from the low 5th class up through 5.11, with the bulk between 5.8 and 5.10. Jellyroll Arch, Pebble in the Sky and Short Cake are among the favorites. Snow shuts the summit in winter, so plan on late spring through fall.
ca_east_face_8.approach: From the lot at the base of School Rock, head north and east past Star Wall toward the lake, cross the open ground and the dry creek bed, and circle the knob to its east side where the slab sits.

ca_cookie_cliff_the.blurb: One of the best-known crack cliffs in the Lower Merced River Canyon below Yosemite Valley, on clean granite beside Highway 140. Nearly all of it is traditional, with splitter cracks and corners, plus a few sport lines and a short top-rope or boulder problem. Grades cluster in the 5.10s and 5.11s, with a good number of 5.12 and a couple of 5.13s. Outer Limits, Catchy, Butterballs and Cookie Monster are among the standouts. Poison oak is common around the base in the canyon, so watch where you step.
ca_cookie_cliff_the.parking_note: Use the pullout on the river side of Highway 140, about half a mile down canyon from the Cascade Creek bridge.
ca_cookie_cliff_the.approach: A short, obvious walk from the pullout to the base of the cliff.

ca_reed_s_pinnacle_2.blurb: A tall granite crag perched above the road near Yosemite Valley, known for long crack and corner routes, from single-pitch to seven-pitch outings. The climbing is mostly traditional with only a small amount of bolted face. Most routes fall at 5.10 and 5.11, with a few easier lines and a couple of 5.12 and 5.13 challenges. The wall catches plenty of sun, which makes it pleasant in cool weather, and the approach is short. Lunatic Fringe and Reed's Pinnacle Regular Route are two of its best-loved climbs.

ca_am_pat_and_jack_pinnacle.blurb: A steep granite crag beside Cascade Falls on the Lower Merced River Canyon, easy to overlook but home to several first-rate trad pitches. Knobs on the wall make the otherwise sustained cracks more approachable, and a few bolted lines sit alongside them. Grades are mostly 5.10 and 5.11, with some 5.12 and a few easier routes. Knob Job, Sherrie's Crack and The Tube are good places to begin. The crag takes lots of sun, which makes it a favorite in fall and winter, and routes tend to dry quickly after a storm.
ca_am_pat_and_jack_pinnacle.parking_note: Park in the pullout or paved lot along Highway 140 near Cascade Falls, west of the Cascade Creek bridge, then cross the road.
ca_am_pat_and_jack_pinnacle.approach: Cross the highway and follow the climbers' trail straight up the hill to the base.

ca_enlightenment_ridge.blurb: A sprawling sandstone boulder field on a gentle slope at Pine Mountain, near 7,000 feet, with wide views over the coast ranges. Problems are scattered over the hillside, and the climbing rewards precise footwork on cracks, faces, arêtes and slopers. Grades run from V0 through the V6 range with one V10 and a few V7s, and the middle grades are especially well stocked. Quiet Soul, Man of Mystery and Enlightenment are among the best known. Landings are often sloped or uneven, so bring several pads and a spotter.
